1.cue: legitimate users not getting valid IP addresses
1.tip: Starvation = the DHCP pool is eaten up, so real users go hungry for addresses.
1.why: In DHCP starvation, an attacker sends many fake requests and leases every address in the pool. Real users then can't get an IP address.

2.tip: Flooding the MAC table? Port security caps how many MACs a port can learn.
2.why: A MAC table overflow attack sends thousands of fake source MACs. Port security limits how many MAC addresses each port may learn, so the table can't fill up.

3.cue: Cisco products focus on endpoint security
3.tip: Endpoints = users' devices. Think what they touch: Web, Email, and NAC (who can join).
3.why: Endpoint security protects hosts. The Web and Email Security Appliances filter what users browse and receive, and NAC checks devices before they join. IPS, VPN and ASA protect the network edge.

4.tip: The supplicant SUPPLIES its credentials: it's the client asking to get in.
4.why: In 802.1X there are three roles: the supplicant (the client), the authenticator (the switch or AP), and the authentication server (usually RADIUS).

5.cue: stores usernames and passwords in the router
5.tip: Stored IN the router = LOCAL. No server, no RADIUS, no TACACS+.
5.why: Local AAA keeps the user database on the router itself. It needs no extra server, which suits small networks. RADIUS and TACACS+ are only used with server-based AAA.

6.tip: CDP and LLDP tell attackers about your gear. Turn them off wherever you don't need them.
6.why: CDP and LLDP advertise device names, models, IOS versions and addresses. An attacker can use that info, so you disable both on interfaces where they aren't needed.

7.cue: mitigate the vulnerability of using Telnet
7.tip: Telnet = plain text. SSH = Secure SHell, encrypted.
7.why: Telnet sends everything, even passwords, in plain text. SSH does the same job of remote management but encrypts the session.

8.tip: Full table = every frame is an unknown unicast, flooded, but only inside its own VLAN.
8.why: When the switch can't learn new MACs, it floods frames like unknown unicasts. VLANs are separate broadcast domains, so the flood stays inside the local VLAN.

9.tip: Supplicant supplies credentials = the client. Switch = authenticator. RADIUS = server.
9.why: The supplicant is the end device asking for network access. The switch is the authenticator, and the authentication server checks the credentials.

10.cue: automatically detect the MAC address of the IP phone and the PC
10.tip: Two devices = maximum 2. Auto-learn into the config = sticky. Leave violation at default (shutdown).
10.why: You must turn on port security, allow 2 MACs (phone and PC) and use sticky so learned MACs go into the running config. The default violation mode is shutdown, which is what the goals want.

11.cue: PC1 is attached to switch S1 with the applied configuration
11.tip: No violation command = default SHUTDOWN mode: port goes err-disabled and logs it.
11.why: The port allows only MAC 000d.bd1b.0245, but PC1 is 000d.bd1b.05ae. That's a violation, and the default mode, shutdown, disables the port and logs a message.

12.cue: designating an unused VLAN as the native VLAN
12.tip: Double-tagging rides the native VLAN. Make the native VLAN unused and the trick fails.
12.why: In double-tagging, the attacker's outer tag matches the native VLAN and gets stripped, so the inner tag sends the frame to another VLAN. An unused native VLAN breaks this.

keys.k: sender MAC address in the ARP body

13.tip: src-mac: compare the Ethernet SOURCE MAC with the ARP SENDER MAC. Source matches sender.
13.why: With validate src-mac, DAI checks that the MAC in the Ethernet header matches the sender MAC inside the ARP message. A mismatch suggests a spoofed ARP, so it's dropped.

14.cue: enable BPDU guard on a switch
14.tip: Global: spanning-tree portfast bpduguard default. Per port: spanning-tree bpduguard enable.
14.why: The global command turns on BPDU guard for all PortFast ports. The interface command turns it on for one port. The other choices are not real IOS syntax.

15.cue: dynamically learned MAC addresses are retained
15.tip: Sticky MACs STICK in the running config, so a saved config keeps them after a reboot.
15.why: Sticky secure MACs are learned on their own but written into the running config. Since the config was saved, the MACs came back after the power outage. Plain dynamic MACs are lost.

16.cue: management frame regularly broadcast by an AP
16.tip: A beacon is like a lighthouse: the AP keeps flashing "I'm here" on a schedule.
16.why: APs send beacon frames regularly to announce their SSID and settings. Probe requests come from clients, and probe responses are only sent as replies.

17.cue: wireless NIC to discover an AP
17.tip: Passive: listen for the beacon. Active: send a probe request.
17.why: In passive mode the client listens for the AP's beacon frames. In active mode the client sends a probe request and the AP answers with a probe response.

18.cue: channel on a wireless router to either 1, 6, or 11
18.tip: 1, 6 and 11 don't overlap in 2.4 GHz. Pick one away from your neighbors.
18.why: In the 2.4 GHz band, only channels 1, 6 and 11 don't overlap. Choosing one that nearby networks aren't using cuts down interference.

19.cue: laptop fails to display any available wireless networks
19.tip: Hidden SSID = no beacons to see. The client must ACTIVELY ask for the network by name.
19.why: No networks show up because the SSID isn't broadcast. The client must use active mode: you type the SSID and it sends probe requests for it.

20.tip: ac = Accelerated: up to 1.3 Gb/s on 5 GHz, still backward compatible.
20.why: 802.11ac reaches about 1.3 Gb/s and works with older 802.11a/n devices. 802.11n tops out around 600 Mb/s, and b and g are much slower.

21.cue: first security measure upon powering up the wireless router
21.tip: First thing: change the default login. Anyone can look up the factory password online.
21.why: Default admin credentials are public. If you don't change them first, anyone can log in and undo every other security setting you make.

22.cue: 3504 WLC dashboard full menu of features
22.tip: Want ALL the features? Click Advanced.
22.why: The WLC opens on a simple Network Summary dashboard. Clicking Advanced in the top right opens the full menu with every setting.

23.cue: before creating a new WLAN on a Cisco 3500 series WLC
23.tip: Each WLAN maps to a VLAN interface. Build the VLAN interface first, then the WLAN.
23.why: A WLAN on the WLC must be tied to an interface so its traffic lands in the right VLAN. So you create the VLAN interface first.

24.cue: 5 Ghz frequency band SSID for streaming media
24.tip: 5 GHz = more lanes on the highway and fewer cars. Good for streaming.
24.why: The 5 GHz band has many more non-overlapping channels and fewer devices using it than 2.4 GHz. Less congestion means better speed for video. Its range is actually shorter.

keys.k: encrypt the messages between the WLC and the RADIUS server

25.tip: The shared secret is shared by WLC and RADIUS only. It protects THEIR talk, not users.
25.why: The WLC and RADIUS server both know the shared secret and use it to secure the messages between them. It isn't a user password.

26.cue: best practices for a home wireless AP
26.tip: Change all the defaults: the SSID, the Wi-Fi password and the AP's admin password.
26.why: Default SSIDs, Wi-Fi keys and admin passwords are well known. Changing all three makes the home network much harder to attack.

27.tip: Authentication = prove WHO you are, with a username and password.
27.why: Authentication checks your identity, usually with a username and password. Authorization and accounting happen after you're logged in.

28.why: 802.11 is the Wi-Fi standard, used for WLANs in homes, offices and campuses on the 2.4 and 5 GHz bands.

29.tip: Starvation uses tons of fake MACs. Port security limits MACs; DHCP snooping limits DHCP messages.
29.why: Port security stops one port from using many fake MAC addresses, and DHCP snooping can rate-limit DHCP messages on untrusted ports. Together they stop the pool from being drained.

keys.k: native VLAN to an unused VLAN

30.tip: Stop VLAN hopping: set trunks by hand, turn off DTP, and park the native VLAN on an unused number.
30.why: VLAN hopping abuses auto trunking (DTP) and the native VLAN. Manual trunks with DTP off stop switch spoofing, and an unused native VLAN stops double-tagging.

31.cue: what can be determined about port security
31.tip: Violation Mode: Shutdown. Shutdown is the default mode.
31.why: The output shows Violation Mode Shutdown, which is the default. The port is Secure-up, not shut down, and only 1 of a maximum of 2 MACs is learned.

32.cue: credentials that will be verified by a server
32.tip: Wi-Fi login checked by a server = RADIUS. AAA is the idea, RADIUS is the server.
32.why: RADIUS is the server protocol that checks wireless users' usernames and passwords. AAA is the overall framework, not a server itself.

33.cue: 802.11n/ac dual-band router to replace the old 802.11g
33.tip: Dual-band router? Split the traffic: old devices on 2.4 GHz, newer ones on 5 GHz.
33.why: Old b/g devices slow down everyone on the 2.4 GHz band. Splitting traffic puts newer devices on 5 GHz so they run at full speed.

34.tip: Microwaves cook at 2.4 GHz, the same as Wi-Fi. That's accidental interference.
34.why: Microwave ovens use the 2.4 GHz frequency and can disrupt Wi-Fi nearby. No one means harm, so it's accidental interference.

35.tip: CAPWAP = the tunnel between the AP and the WLC. Think: AP to controller.
35.why: CAPWAP lets a controller manage lightweight APs. It wraps up and carries user traffic and control messages between the AP and the WLC. It uses UDP, not TCP.

36.cue: Match each functional component of AAA

keys.k: proves that users are who they say

36.tip: AAA: Authentication = who are you? Authorization = what can you do? Accounting = what did you do?
36.why: Authentication checks identity, authorization decides what you may access, and accounting logs what you did. Billing for remote access is not one of the AAA functions here.

37.cue: authenticate users against a central database
37.tip: The two AAA servers: TACACS+ (Cisco) and RADIUS (open standard).
37.why: Server-based AAA uses TACACS+ or RADIUS to check users against a central database. SSH and HTTPS are for secure access, not the AAA lookup.

38.cue: result of a DHCP starvation attack
38.tip: Starvation = no addresses left to eat. Rogue server lies = DHCP spoofing.
38.why: The attacker leases every address in the pool, so real clients can't get one. Handing out bad gateway or DNS info is a different attack: DHCP spoofing.

39.tip: Double-tagging needs the attacker's VLAN to equal the trunk's native VLAN.
39.why: The switch strips the outer tag only when it matches the native VLAN. If the attacker sits in that same VLAN, the inner tag carries the frame into another VLAN.

40.cue: track individuals who access network resources
40.tip: Accounting = keeping the books: who did what, and when.
40.why: Accounting records what users access and what changes they make, so you can audit it later.

41.cue: How many ports among switches should be assigned as trusted
41.tip: Trust the uplinks toward the server plus the server's own port: 6 uplinks + 1 server port = 7.
41.why: DHCP replies must be trusted on paths toward the server. Each access switch has 2 uplinks to DS1 and DS2 (6 ports), plus the AS3 port to the DHCP server makes 7.

42.tip: Port security default = SHUTDOWN (err-disabled). Strictest is the default.
42.why: Unless you change it, a port security violation puts the port into err-disabled, so it shuts down and logs it.

43.cue: laptop cannot connect to a wireless access point
43.tip: Start simple: is Wi-Fi turned on? Did you pick the right network?
43.why: The quickest checks are the basics: that the wireless NIC is turned on and that the laptop is joining the correct SSID.

44.tip: Cloaked SSID = hidden name. Users must type it in, but sniffers can still find it.
44.why: With cloaking, the AP stops advertising the SSID, so users must enter it by hand. It's weak security, because the SSID still shows up in other frames.

45.tip: Personal = one shared password. Enterprise = each user checked by RADIUS.
45.why: WPA2/WPA3 Enterprise uses 802.1X with a RADIUS server so each user logs in with their own credentials. Personal mode uses one pre-shared key.

46.tip: Slow dual-band Wi-Fi? Split the traffic across 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz.
46.why: 802.11n can use both bands. Putting some devices on 5 GHz and others on 2.4 GHz spreads the load and reduces crowding.

47.tip: SNMP: the M is for Management and Monitoring.
47.why: SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) lets a manager collect stats and alerts from network devices.

48.tip: Private 10.x address to the internet? NAT translates it.
48.why: 10.0.10.0/24 is a private range that can't go on the internet. NAT translates those addresses to the router's public address.

49.cue: voice and video data are prioritized
49.tip: Priority for voice and video = Quality of Service.
49.why: QoS puts time-sensitive traffic like voice and video ahead of email and web traffic, so calls and streams don't stutter.

50.why: 802.1X is port-based access control built on those three roles: the client, the switch or AP, and the RADIUS server.

51.tip: Size order: PAN < LAN < MAN < WAN. Global = WAN.
51.why: A WWAN covers the largest areas, such as countries or the globe, often using cellular or satellite links.

52.cue: Which feature on a switch makes it vulnerable to VLAN hopping
52.tip: VLAN hopping uses DTP: ports that auto-negotiate a trunk let attackers become a trunk.
52.why: With auto trunking (DTP) on, an attacker's device can pretend to be a switch and form a trunk, getting access to all VLANs.

53.cue: which resources a user can access
53.tip: Authorization = what are you ALLOWED to do?
53.why: After you log in, authorization decides which resources you can reach and which commands you can run.

54.tip: Static secure MAC + different PC = violation = shutdown.
54.why: Only MAC 0023.189d.6456 is allowed on Fa0/2. A workstation with a different MAC is a violation, and the default mode shuts the port down.

55.tip: limit rate 6 = at most 6 DHCP discovery messages per second on each port.
55.why: The rate limit stops a port from flooding DHCP discovers, as in a starvation attack. Each of ports Fa0/5 to Fa0/10 can receive up to 6 per second.

56.cue: dropped and no notification should be sent
56.tip: Protect is the quiet one: drops, no log. Restrict drops AND logs. Shutdown kills the port.
56.why: Protect mode silently drops frames from unknown MACs. Restrict also drops them but sends a log message and counts it.

57.cue: simple way to achieve a split-the-traffic result
57.tip: Split the traffic = give each band its own SSID, so devices pick a band.
57.why: Using a different SSID for 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz lets users and devices choose a band on purpose, which spreads out the traffic.

58.tip: What you CAN DO = authorization. Who you are = authentication.
58.why: Authorization sets the permissions for each user, such as which commands or resources they may use.

59.cue: wireless access to a city or district
59.why: A WMAN covers a city or district, larger than a building LAN but smaller than a WAN.

60.cue: configure a WLAN for a specific security option such as WPA2
60.tip: WPA2 for a WLAN? Edit it under the WLANs tab.
60.why: Each WLAN's settings, including its security mode like WPA2, are edited on the WLANs tab. The SECURITY tab is for things like RADIUS servers.

61.cue: large open spaces, such as hallways
61.tip: Omni = all. An omnidirectional antenna spreads signal in all directions.
61.why: An omnidirectional antenna sends signal all around it, which covers open rooms and hallways. Yagi and dish antennas focus signal in one direction.

62.cue: BPDU guard on PortFast enabled interfaces
62.tip: PortFast ports are for PCs. If a BPDU shows up, a switch was plugged in: BPDU guard shuts it down.
62.why: End devices don't send BPDUs. If a PortFast port gets one, a switch was connected, so BPDU guard disables the port to keep rogue switches out.

63.tip: Logs of commands = accounting, the record book.
63.why: Accounting keeps a record of what users did, including the commands they entered.

64.cue: coverage over an extensive geographic area
64.why: A WWAN uses transmitters such as cell towers to cover very large areas, much bigger than a city.

65.cue: controls who is permitted to access a network
65.tip: WHO gets in = authentication. WHAT they do = authorization.
65.why: Authentication checks your identity before you get access to the network.

66.cue: operate only in the 5 GHz range
66.tip: Only 5 GHz: a and ac. b and g are 2.4 GHz, n uses both, ad is 60 GHz.
66.why: 802.11a and 802.11ac use only the 5 GHz band. 802.11b and g use 2.4 GHz, 802.11n can use both, and 802.11ad uses 60 GHz.

67.tip: Personal = around you, just a few feet: WPAN.
67.why: A WPAN uses low-power radios like Bluetooth to connect devices close to one person.

68.cue: wireless network for an entire college building
68.tip: Building-wide Wi-Fi = infrastructure mode, with APs on the wired network.
68.why: Infrastructure mode uses APs connected to the wired network so clients can roam across the building. Ad hoc is just devices linking to each other.

69.why: A WMAN covers a city or large urban area.

70.cue: suitable for use in a home or office
70.why: A WLAN covers a home, office or campus using Wi-Fi.

71.tip: Asking for a service? Authorization answers PASS or FAIL: are you allowed?
71.why: When a user requests a service, authorization checks their permissions and replies PASS (allowed) or FAIL (not allowed).

72.tip: Antennas on rooftops across a city = WMAN.
72.why: A WMAN often links sites across a city using antennas mounted on buildings.

73.why: Accounting collects data on what users did and how long, which can be used for audits or billing.

74.why: A WLAN covers a medium area like a building, roughly up to 300 feet from the AP.

75.cue: audits what users actions are performed
75.why: Accounting records users' actions so they can be audited later.

76.tip: Bluetooth headset, ZigBee sensor = short range = WPAN.
76.why: Bluetooth and ZigBee are low-power, short-range radios used for personal-area networks.

77.cue: implemented either locally or as a server-based
77.tip: Local AAA or server-based AAA: both are ways to do authentication.
77.why: Authentication can use a local user database on the device or a central server like RADIUS or TACACS+.

keys.k: 2.4 GHz band for basic internet traffic

78.tip: Split the traffic: 5 GHz for fast, time-sensitive media. 2.4 GHz for everyday browsing.
78.why: Splitting the traffic means putting streaming and time-sensitive traffic on the faster, less crowded 5 GHz band and basic internet use on 2.4 GHz.

79.cue: restricts LAN access through publicly accessible switch ports
79.tip: Public switch port? 802.1X makes devices log in before the port lets traffic through.
79.why: 802.1X blocks traffic on a switch port until the connected device is authenticated, so anyone plugging into a public port can't get on the LAN.
